HI-2026-HB2021.title: RELATING TO TRANSPORTATION.
HI-2026-HB2021.summary: Establishes safe riding behaviors for electric bicycles. Prohibits the operation of high-speed electric devices in certain locations. Establishes labeling and signage requirements for electric bicycles. Prohibits the operation of a moped or electric motorcycle in certain locations. Amends the definition of "bicycle" for purposes of county vehicular taxes. Defines "electric bicycle" in place of "low-speed electric bicycle". Authorizes the seizure of non-road-legal or nonconforming electric bicycles and high-speed electric devices. Defines "electric micro-mobility device" and requires the same regulations as electric foot scooters. Prohibits a person under the age of sixteen from operating a class 2 or class 3 electric bicycle without direct supervision. Authorizes a person to ride an electric bicycle on a sidewalk under certain circumstances. Prohibits a person from operating a bicycle or electric foot scooter under the age of eighteen without a helmet. Repeals the requirement that moped drivers use bicycle lanes. Substitutes the term "motor scooter" with the term "motor-driven cycle". (CD1)

HI-2026-HB2021.aiSummary: Creates new riding rules for electric bicycles and other small electric devices in Hawaii. It limits where some high-speed electric devices, mopeds, and electric motorcycles can be used, adds label and sign rules, and requires helmets for riders under 18. It also lets counties tax bicycles under a new definition and changes some terms used in state law.

actions.text: Received.

HI-2026-GM1345.aiSummary: The measure became Act 243 and is called the Hawaii Braille Literacy Education Act. It requires the state education department to provide braille instruction and braille learning materials for eligible students with low vision or blindness when certain conditions are met. It also sets out braille literacy support services, information sharing with the human services department, and work on section 504 plans and individualized education programs.

HI-2026-GM1336.title: Informing the Legislature that on July 13, 2026, the Governor signed the following bill into law: HB1888 HD3 SD2 CD1 (ACT 234).

actions.text: Received.

HI-2026-GM1336.aiSummary: Signed into law on July 13, 2026, this act would add new protections for Department of Education and state public charter school workers, including sports officials. It would require schools to have steps for reporting and handling harassment, make yearly safety training, and create written safety plans for harmful situations. It would also allow paid leave for court dates tied to harassment cases and let the attorney general help workers seek a temporary restraining order, with some reimbursement for serving papers but not lawyer or court fees.

HI-2026-GM1330.title: Informing the Legislature that on July 10, 2026, the Governor signed the following bill into law: SB2247 SD1 HD1 CD1 (ACT 228).

actions.text: Received.

HI-2026-GM1330.aiSummary: Signed into law as Act 228, the measure bars certain top Hawaii executive branch employees from going to political fundraisers or asking for campaign donations. It applies to employees appointed by the governor to paid jobs that need Senate confirmation, while they hold that covered job. The law says they may still vote, make personal political donations, and share political views as private people.

HI-2026-GM1327.aiSummary: The governor signed this measure into law as Act 225. It changes Hawaii law on bribery and sets a nine-year time limit to start a bribery case. It also says someone convicted of bribery cannot use a deferred plea deal.

HI-2026-GM1321.title: Informing the Legislature that on July 9, 2026, the Governor signed the following bill into law: HB1969 HD2 SD1 CD1 (ACT 219).

actions.text: Received.

HI-2026-GM1321.aiSummary: The law sets up state-funded help for colorectal cancer screenings and, for uninsured residents who need it after a screening, treatment too. It also says some health plans must cover these screenings and follow-up colonoscopies without deductibles or other cost sharing. The state will spend $1,800,000 for fiscal year 2026-2027 to run the program, and it takes effect on July 1, 2026.
